title: Political strategist on how Trump's personal grievances could affect the GOP
description: NPR's Steve Inskeep speaks with political strategist and former senior Republican congressional adviser Rina Shah about how President Trump's p
body:
NPR's Steve Inskeep speaks with political strategist and former senior Republican congressional adviser Rina Shah about how President Trump's personal grievances and projects are affecting the chances of GOP candidates in the upcoming election.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    MICHEL MARTIN, HOST:  Rina Shah has been listening with us. She is a political strategist with experience as a GOP congressional adviser. Good morning, Rina.RINA SHAH: Hi. Good morning.MARTIN: So Mara mentioned the president's complaints, and in some cases, moves against people like Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook, the media, the government of Norway. Is - does any of that motivate voters at this point, either in his base or independents?SHAH: Well, I think it's really important to see what this really is. The diesel deal and the energy ceasefire announcement, I believe, are less about immediate relief and more about creating a permission structure for Republican candidates. The volumes are really too small to meaningfully move prices before November 3. I think most analysts are saying that plainly, and most of us kind of get that.But the move lets candidates say that the president is trying something on cost instead of doing nothing. And that's really the narrow political utility here. The risk is that Zelenskyy's criticism and then the lack of clear details on the ceasefire turn it into another foreign policy story that down-ballot Republicans then have to explain rather than use.MARTIN: But also it doesn't work. It doesn't seem to be working. He's saying one thing, and the facts prove to be otherwise. And to that end, you know, the president's defending - he's aggressively defended his decision to launch trade wars with much of the world, his military war with Iran. Those are both things that have raised prices for Americans. The latest NPR/PBS News/Marist poll indicates that independent voters favor Democrats by 19 points on the economy. So the question is, you're saying, even if it creates a permission structure, does that - is that enough?SHAH: Well, look, let's look at the broader midterm picture here. Trump is running the same play he always has - make every race about himself and then bet that his base's intensity outweighs his approval numbers, which we know are pretty dismal. The difference this cycle is that the grievances that are driving a lot of the White House's agenda - which are media fights, the Department of Justice's action against people from the first term, his personal score-settling - those are more self-generated than they were in 2016 or '18. Back then, a larger share of what he amplified tracked the existing voter frustration.Now more of it originates from inside the administration, and it's getting projected outward, and that really changes the utility for candidates. It motivates the core base, but it doesn't give swing voters a new reason to show up when their main concern is still the price of diesel and groceries. But I'd be remiss if I didn't mention here the practical problem for Republicans in these next three weeks, and it's that there is not a clean off-ramp for them. Candidates in really tight races would prefer a more narrow message on things like border enforcement and costs, and the White House is not structured at all to deliver that.Trump treats the midterms as an extension of his own presidency rather than a set of local races, which is really unusual, even by our modern standards. Presidents have always campaigned, but they have rarely, rarely made themselves the constant central character this late while the party is trailing on the economy. And what that does is forces candidates to either fully nationalize their races or spend time creating distance, and neither of which is ideal with three weeks left.MARTIN: Sure. So if the president can't or won't focus his message on what voters care about right now, and if there doesn't seem to be anybody in the president's circle who can get him to do that, is there anything that congressional candidates can do?SHAH: Oh, that is the question du jour. Look, three weeks out, it's very hard for anyone to redirect him. He sets the agenda. The people closest to him can sometimes influence timing or emphasis on a particular issue like prices, but they rarely change his overall focus or stop him from going where he wants to go. At this point in the midterm cycle, I think the political reality of the map and the polls can sometimes force a more narrow message. But that's really different, again, from someone inside Trump world circle - they're successfully shifting him.I would say this - look, if the polls are right and Republicans are trailing on the broad economy or the cost-of-living question, the other issues that can still drive their turnout are the border and public safety. Those have consistently been stronger for Republicans in recent cycles, and they give candidates a concrete contrast - things like enforcement, resources and results, versus what they argue has been a more permissive Democratic policy.MARTIN: OK, before we let you go through...SHAH: Also energy domestic production.MARTIN: Thirty seconds left, though. Republicans...SHAH: SureMARTIN: ...A big campaign bank. Republicans are outspending Democrats in these final weeks. Do they have - is that enough to erase some of these Democratic advantages that we're seeing in the polls?SHAH: Truly, I don't believe so. I think right now, what we're looking at is a real downside because what's emanating from the White House has created that. The downside here to Trump's strategy so far is that it's locked the midterms into a pure referendum on him. And look, by inserting himself constantly and tying every race to his record and grievances, he's made it really hard for vulnerable Republicans to run as independent of Washington. And in a cycle where his approval is low and prices remain high, that nationalizes races in a way that often favors the out-party...MARTIN: OK.SHAH: ...Which is the Democrats.MARTIN: That is Republican political strategist Rina Shah. Rina, thanks.SHAH: Thank you.

title: New White House press secretary a 'devoted fan' of Trump and MAGA
body:
Katie Zacharia, pictured on Dec. 14, 2025, in Franklin, Tenn., starts her tenure as White House press secretary.
                
                    Terry Wyatt/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Terry Wyatt/Getty Images
    

   
   President Trump's new White House press secretary Katie Zacharia is expected to take the podium on Tuesday for her first press briefing. Zacharia steps in as Trump's chief spokesperson at a moment when his popularity has fallen to record lows and Republicans are scrambling to limit potential losses in the midterm elections.   The Trump administration is also engaged in a legal battle with the press corps that work to cover Trump. Last month, the White House restricted access by CNN, MS NOW and Politico, news organizations that Trump views as unfriendly. The Justice Department has since launched an investigation into the five television networks that share pool video coverage of Trump.   
   In a post on social media, Zacharia, an attorney and a mother of four, offered no hint of the challenges ahead. She described her new job as the "honor of a lifetime" and praised Trump's policies. "His confidence is a true privilege, and his leadership is a blessing to this country," Zacharia wrote on Friday.   In naming Zacharia, Trump praised her longstanding personal loyalty. "She has an unblemished record of support, and has been a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning," Trump said. "She is, likewise, a devoted fan and member of MAGA!"   Zacharia, 41, a graduate of Pepperdine Caruso School of Law, has worked for a number of conservative organizations, according to her online resume. She served on the advisory board for an anti-abortion group called The White Rose Resistance that took its name from Christian students who challenged the Nazis. White Rose says it's working to counter "the same evils, the same apathy" faced by opponents of the Nazi regime.   More recently, Zacharia has served as a communications advisor for the Trump Media & Technology Group, the firm that operates Trump's Truth Social platform. She has also been a frequent pro-Trump commentator on conservative outlets including Fox News and Newsmax.   
   During an appearance in August on the network Real America's Voice, Zacharia weighed in on the Lindsay Clancy murder trial, arguing that "toxic feminism" had skewed the public's view of the case. Clancy was charged with killing her three children. The five-week trial ended in a mistrial after sparking a national conversation over postpartum depression.   "This started with the advocation of abortion," Zacharia said. "When women are championing the death and murder and the ability to murder their children from conception all the way through, when does humanity begin and end?"   Zacharia has also used her social media posts to amplify right-wing conspiracy theories, including claims that Democratic leaders took part in pedophile rings. In one post from 2022, she described former Democratic White House chief of staff John Podesta as "Pedo Podesta." That same year she shared a post from a far-right commentator who claimed Democrats "want to mask and rape your children."   NPR asked the White House for comment on the posts, which were first uncovered by the online progressive media site Popular Information. Administration officials responded in an email by praising Zacharia without addressing her social media comments.   After being named to serve as White House press secretary, Zacharia drew praise from other administration officials. FBI Director Kash Patel described her as "sharp, fearless" and someone who "knows what it means to stand for the American people."   Karoline Leavitt, who held the press secretary post until August before stepping down, also praised Zacharia. "I have no doubt Katie will do great work for President Trump and our country," she said on X.   In an appearance on Fox News on Saturday, Zacharia boosted Trump's controversial plan to import Russian diesel fuel, which has drawn bipartisan criticism. She also praised Trump's efforts to rally GOP support ahead of the November vote, while suggesting congressional Republicans may be to blame for any losses.   
   "President Trump has made the case and delivered historic results. I would have loved to see more from our congressional Republicans and Senate," she said.

title: Government spent $10 million on pro-Trump ads after president said super PAC would fund
description: President Trump leaves the stage after s
body:
President Trump leaves the stage after speaking during an election rally in Syracuse, New York on Oct. 9, 2026.
                
                    Alex Wong/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Alex Wong/Getty Images
    

   
   Ads promoting President Trump and his policies continued to be paid for by the U.S. government well after Trump announced he would have his MAGA Inc. super PAC take over funding the ads and kept airing despite a federal judge ordering them to come down.   An NPR analysis of data from AdImpact finds that nearly $22 million in taxpayer dollars has been spent to air the ads since the campaign began in late September. Nearly $10 million of that total was spent after Oct. 5, when the president pledged to fund it privately in a post on Truth Social.   
   "The Radical Left is upset with the fact that I am taking Ads, which I consider to be a positive promotion for our Great U.S.A., and paying for them with U.S.A. money," Trump posted at the time. "This is a rather standard thing to do but, rather than doing that, although nothing will make them happy, I have decided to do the Patriotic Ads, among others, and pay for them myself, and with money I raised for MAGA, Inc."   The ads have been criticized by lawmakers on both sides of the aisle with Republicans praising the president's choice to shift funding for the ads to an outside super PAC. But, that praise was premature. Despite giving the impression that there'd been a policy change, the government-funded ads didn't stop airing after Trump's post.   The White House has repeatedly referred to the ads as public service announcements, but a lawsuit filed by Common Cause and others argued they were being funded without congressional approval and violated restrictions on publicity and propaganda produced with taxpayer dollars.   The ads — five of them in all — cover a wide range of pro-Trump content. One includes a splashy montage of photos of the president with a chorus singing "love me" serving as the soundtrack. Another is an exact duplicate of an ad made by the Trump campaign during the 2024 election cycle. Two promote the military operations in Venezuela and Iran. All of them end with the words "Paid for by the U.S. Government" on the screen.   
   The spots continued being broadcast for several hours after a federal judge overseeing the lawsuit issued a temporary ruling Sunday night saying the government "shall cancel or cause to be cancelled any slot, placement, reservation, or arrangement for the airing or dissemination of the challenged advertisements, including those placements for the evening of October 11, 2026."   Pro-Trump spots aired hundreds of additional times Sunday night into the wee hours of Monday morning.   "The last PSAs paid for by the government aired yesterday evening," a White House official not authorized to speak publicly told NPR on Monday afternoon, adding that the government "did not receive notice from the court in time to cancel the ad buys. The PSAs will be paid for by outside groups moving forward."   The White House had previously said that taxpayer funds used for ads would not be reimbursed. The White House has also insisted these ads were merely about promoting patriotism. They argued the ads can't be campaign related because the president isn't running for office this year and have nothing to do with the midterm elections next month. But Trump has repeatedly implored voters to vote like he is on the ballot and his dismal approval ratings have been dragging down Republicans all over the country.   A recent Reuters/Ipsos poll found the ads are pretty unpopular. The poll asked whether it is appropriate or inappropriate to use "taxpayer funds to pay for election-related television ads featuring the President or members of his cabinet." It wasn't even close, with 86% of Americans saying it is inappropriate. Even 80% of Republicans said the ads were inappropriate.   It's rare to get such bipartisan agreement on anything these days.

title: Win or lose, independent candidates want to meet voters in the middle
description: Alaska U.S. House candidate Bill Hill, a
body:
Alaska U.S. House candidate Bill Hill, an independent, poses in a park in downtown Juneau, Alaska, on June 4, 2026.
                
                    Becky Bohrer/AP
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Becky Bohrer/AP
    

   
   These days, Seth Haskin often puts on a puff-sleeved linen shirt under an 18th century waistcoat, breeches fastened just below the knee, long socks and buckle shoes that make a distinctive clip-clop when he walks.   The outfit is meant to remind people of the Founding Fathers and evoke their idea of limited government, which the 26-year-old supports.   Haskin's day job is managing his family's coffee shop business but this year he's been vying for another position: independent congressional representative for Southwest Florida. While campaigning, Haskin also carries an old-school bell.   "Getting their [people's] attention is the biggest battle that most candidates have," Haskin said. "But especially independent or no party candidates."   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Independent congressional candidate Seth Haskin in Naples, Fla., posing for his campaign on Sept. 3 in his typical outfit of a puff-sleeved linen shirt under an 18th century waistcoat.
                
                    Tyler Haskin/Seth Haskin for Congress
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Tyler Haskin/Seth Haskin for Congress
    

   
   Some could dismiss Haskin's attire as a stunt, and they may write off other independent candidates the same way. Sarah Zabel, 61, an independent candidate for Idaho's western district, said that view is outdated.   
   "Independents used to be a curiosity or a protest or a single issue," said Zabel. "Now, with the parties having gone to such extremes, independents are the necessary relief for the American voter."   At a time when 45 percent of adults identify as political independents — a record high — and just a handful of tight races will decide control of Congress, the 173 independents running for the House this fall will test how big the political middle really is, and whether people who identify as independents will vote for one.   Despite the significant chunk of Americans identifying as independents, right now just one independent serves in the House: Kevin Kiley. The congressman whose newly redrawn California district leans Democratic, switched from Republican to independent while in Congress and continues to caucus with Republicans, reported Politico.   Some candidates said they were always independent, others said their political beliefs didn't change, but their parties did. While some are confident about winning, others said even a double-digit share of the vote will show both parties that it's time for change.   Providing an alternative    Zabel, who is running in a deep-red district in Idaho, describes herself as a "heritage Republican," or someone who used to be a Republican and adheres to conservative values. But since 2018, during the first Trump administration, she stopped feeling in line with the Republican party and the "MAGA program."   
   The retired Air Force major general said she didn't feel represented by either party, and she soon learned that many of her neighbors felt the same way.   "That's why I decided that I would step forward and be a candidate from the center," Zabel said. "Idaho is more Republican than Democrat, it is more conservative than not. But the extremes you see, they are a minority."   The Cook Political Report rates the district, which voted for Trump by a 45-point landslide in 2024, as solid Republican for the incumbent, Rep. Russ Fulcher.    
   Zabel, who noted that she would not caucus with either party if in Congress, recognizes that the Democratic nominee narrows her path to victory, but Zabel sees value "in showing Idaho and showing the country that we aren't the MAGA stronghold."   In Colorado, Shimon Blau, a lifelong independent, did not intend to run for Congress. Until Melat Kiros, 29, won the Democratic nomination for the state's 1st Congressional District, which encompasses the solidly Democratic city of Denver.   "I was deeply disturbed by the results of the primaries in which our 30-year incumbent, Diana DeGette, was beat by a member of the Democratic Socialists of America," he said. "I was offended and bothered by [Kiros'] past antisemitic rhetoric, as well as a lot of her socialist beliefs."   Kiros faced wide criticism in June for declining to describe a 2025 fatal firebombing attack on Jewish activists in Boulder, Colo., as antisemitic. Blau, the Denver-based physician, received an endorsement from The Denver Gazette on Oct. 6; it described him as the "candidate of conscience."   Kiros' upset of DeGette propelled Blau to swiftly gather the 1,500 signatures he needed to be eligible to run as an independent. Blau believes that in a city as blue as Denver, Republicans are "more of the message candidate than independents," with the latter having a real chance at winning.   
   "I think there's a lot of disillusionment right now with both parties," he said. "It seems like both of our traditional parties are leaning more and more towards the extremes."   Seth Haskin from Florida is also running in a district where one party has dominated for years. Trump won at least 60 percent of the vote in the past two presidential elections in Haskin's district, and local media mogul Jim Schwartzel won a tight and crowded Republican primary in August with almost 30 percent of the vote.    
   A "strict constitutionalist," Haskin, who previously also ran for governor of Wisconsin as a write-in candidate, said he could've seen himself in either party before the Covid-19 pandemic, before he believed that both parties had been "captured by the same industry leaders and PAC money and foreign lobbies and everything else."   Now, he's running as an independent because he thinks voters are ready for a change.   "Even if I don't win, if I can get double-digit percentage points as an independent candidate, I will get a lot of phone calls from both parties," he said. "It's going to threaten the duopoly that they have, right?"   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                In this undated photo from the campaign, independent congressional candidate Sarah Zabel campaigns with community members in Grangeville, Idaho.
                
                    Shireene Hale/Zabel for Congress
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Shireene Hale/Zabel for Congress
    

   
   Independents in swing districts   In competitive swing districts like Iowa's 1st and states with ranked-choice voting like Alaska, independents aren't campaigning on the idea that both parties have gone too far, but that neither is delivering.   Businessman Michael Bridgford is running as an independent against Republican Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks and Christina Bohannan, the Democratic nominee and former state representative.   The Cook Political Report, which long had the race as a toss-up, recently rated the district as lean Democratic.   Bridgford said people are tired of the "dysfunction" from both parties and by watching Miller-Meeks and Bohannan compete, and they believe that independents can provide the stable center that will let the government solve problems.   
   Running in a swing district has some advantages for independents.    
   "People are more independent minded. It's not gerrymandered to one side," Bridgford said. "People are more middle of the road and so there's naturally more attraction to this type of campaign."   The challenge is competing against the money that parties typically pour into a competitive district, he said.   In Alaska, even though voters have almost always picked the Republican presidential nominee, their streak of independence has allowed independents and Democratic nominees to win statewide races.   Bill Hill, a commercial fisherman who said he registered as an independent when he was 18, has decided to take his chances in Alaska's at-large congressional race, rated as a likely Republican win. Hill said, like many other Alaskans, he doesn't fit into a political box.   "People who are registered Republicans often have some progressive viewpoints and people registered as Democrats may have more conservative viewpoints as well," he said. "Alaskans just don't toe a political line with every vote."   Like other independents, Hill lauds that independents can work for their constituents without worrying about leadership in Washington. He's competing against the Republican incumbent Nick Begich, the Democratic nominee Eric Hafner and Jim McDermott, a Libertarian.   Hill, who was about 12 points behind Begich in the primary, also has an offer of support from the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, according to Anchorage Daily News.   Independent candidates throughout the country are running for a variety of reasons and facing challenges including fundraising and finding debate platforms with party candidates, but what unites them and keeps them going is their belief in the power of the moderate middle.   "When you talk to enough people and they're all moderate and everybody they know is moderate, but they believe everybody they don't know must be right wing," said Sarah Zabel, the independent candidate from Idaho. "You see that it's just an illusion. And we can bust that illusion."

title: Government spent millions on Trump ads. And, federal agents raid Ilhan Omar's home
description: Trump Midterm Campaigning, Rep. Omar Home Searched, Europe Pushes Back on Russia Deal
body:
Trump Midterm Campaigning, Rep. Omar Home Searched, Europe Pushes Back on Russia Deal
    
            
                
                Transcript

      Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.   Today's top stories   The U.S. government continues to pay for ads promoting President Trump, even after he announced that his MAGA Inc. super PAC would take over funding. A federal judge ordered the ads to be taken down, yet they remained on air. An NPR analysis of data from AdImpact finds that nearly $22 million in taxpayer funds have been spent since the campaign began in late September. Almost $10 million of that was spent after Trump pledged on an Oct. 5 Truth Social post to fund the campaign privately. The White House has called the ads public service announcements, but a lawsuit by Common Cause and others argued they were funded without congressional approval, violating restrictions on taxpayer-funded publicity and propaganda.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                President Trump leaves the stage after speaking during an election rally in Syracuse, New York on Oct. 9, 2026.
                
                    Alex Wong/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Alex Wong/Getty Images
    

   
   Trump has ramped up his campaign travel ahead of the midterm elections. He rallied supporters in Youngstown, Ohio, last night and is heading to Alaska today. More events are planned for later this week. He has been trying to encourage his supporters to vote by telling them to pretend he is on the ballot.   
   🎧 Trump's events resemble his presidential campaign rallies: He emphasizes his accomplishments while calling out superfans and insulting Democrats, NPR's Danielle Kurtzleben tells Up First. Kurtzleben adds that Trump's campaign trail emphasizes that the GOP is still his party, despite his declining approval. Candidates like Ohio GOP gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy and GOP Sen. Jon Husted saw large, appreciative, but Kurtzleben says the benefits of appearing alongside Trump remain unclear.➡️ With just weeks until Election Day, polls may start to flood the landscape. While they serve as a helpful tool, remember they can't predict the future. Keep these tips in mind as polls pour in.➡️ The NPR App has all of NPR's election coverage in one place — from the biggest stories across the country, to the issues that matter close to home. Browse headlines, playlists, podcast episodes, videos and more, all on the 2026 Election tab.   Federal agents searched Rep. Ilhan Omar's home in Washington, D.C., yesterday morning. Omar, D-Minn., says the search was politically motivated by the Trump administration. The Department of Justice told NPR in a statement that Homeland Security Investigations agents "executed a judicially authorized search warrant," approved by the DOJ, as part of an ongoing federal investigation. Current and former federal officials with knowledge of the search who were not authorized to speak publicly confirmed the details, revealing that this multi-year probe includes whistleblower complaints and focuses on allegations of immigration fraud.   
   🎧 One of Omar's neighbors, 79-year-old Sharon Jackson, tells NPR's Luke Garrett she was awoken yesterday at around 4:30 a.m. by loud knocking and that vans and agents wearing gloves were walking to and from the congresswoman's house. Vice President JD Vance previously accused Omar of immigration fraud, which she denies. Omar is an American citizen who left Somalia as a refugee. She stated on social media that the president has spent a decade targeting her with smear campaigns and vowed not to be silenced. Trump says that he is not involved in the investigation into Omar.   Living better   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                The safest way to protect yourself from measles when traveling is to be vaccinated.
                
                    Malte Mueller/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Malte Mueller/Getty Images
    

   
   Living Better is a special series about what it takes to stay healthy in America.   The U.S. is experiencing its worst measles resurgence in decades. More than 3,600 confirmed cases and two deaths have been reported as of late September. Outbreaks in several states and exposures in public places like bars, sports stadiums and public transit have raised concerns about travel safety. Almost all U.S. measles cases involve unvaccinated individuals, and as the outbreaks grow in some states, the risk of exposure is getting higher. Here's what to know before traveling by plane or train.   ✈️ People who've had two doses of the MMR vaccine are considered protected against measles.✈️ The disease is highly contagious. It spreads through the air when an infected person coughs, breathes or sneezes. That airspace can remain contaminated for up to two hours.✈️ Check with your healthcare provider about your vaccination status. They may recommend a booster based on your medical history and health.✈️ Immunocompromised individuals may be unable to receive vaccination and often rely on herd immunity for protection. For measles, the vaccination threshold for herd immunity is 95%.✈️ Measles can be hard to track because symptoms — such as fever, cough, and rash — typically appear seven to 14 days after exposure and can sometimes take long as 21 days to surface.   
   Picture show   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                When Lee Krasner was asked in a 1978 interview what she was doing while her husband Jackson Pollock was becoming so famous, she said, "I was working all the time." Krasner is shown above, at work, in 1981.
                
                    Ernst Haas/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Ernst Haas/Getty Images
    

   
   The Metropolitan Museum of Art's new blockbuster exhibition showcases the works of two 20th-century artists. Jackson Pollock is well-known for his drip paintings. His wife, Lee Krasner, has often been overshadowed by her husband. This show finally gives Krasner the recognition she deserves. With more than 120 pieces on display — 74 from Krasner and 48 from Pollock — the show highlights Krasner as a titan of Abstract Expressionism, too. Check out some of the photos from the exhibit.   3 things to know before you go   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                U.S. economists Robert E. Hall and Michael Woodford are announced as the winners of the 2026 Nobel prize in economics at the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm on Monday.
                
                    Jonathan Nackstrand/AFP via Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Jonathan Nackstrand/AFP via Getty Images
    

   
   Americans Robert Hall from Stanford University and Michael Woodford from Columbia University have won the Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences for their work on managing boom-and-bust cycles to reduce inflation and unemployment.Trump's new press secretary, Katie Zacharia, will hold her first press briefing today. She has raised her profile by appearing on conservative outlets and promoting right-wing conspiracy theories.Hectic early-morning traffic can make breakfast a luxury in Lagos, Nigeria. Akara is a roadside staple. For NPR's Breakfast Around the World series, Emmanuel Akinwotu explores the savory snack's deep roots in Nigeria and West Africa, and its spread around the world during the trans-Atlantic slave trade.   This newsletter was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.

title: Polls are a snapshot, and other helpful things to remember during the midterm elections
description: Residents line up to cast their early-vo
body:
Residents line up to cast their early-voting ballots in Arlington, Va., on Sept. 18, the first day of early voting in the state.
                
                    Tom Brenner/Getty Images
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Tom Brenner/Getty Images
    

   
   This is about the time of year when the country engages in the Great American Biennial Polling Freakout.   A few weeks before an election, lots of people start to really engage. They read headlines showing this candidate or that candidate leading a race. People wonder who's going to win and whether the polls are right or wrong. And it all often leads to a blend of anticipation mixed with confusion and anxiety.   Stop and breathe. All that needs to be known from the polls at this point is that over the last several months, the compass needle has moved more in Democrats' direction. That's it. They are the favorites to win the House and are within striking distance of winning the Senate, something that was seen as a long shot when this election cycle began.    
   That's based not just on the polls but on conversations with campaigns and on-the-ground reporting. But here are some tips and things to remember as the deluge of polls comes your way:   1. Polls are not meant to be predictive.    They are snapshots in time of when those surveys were conducted.   2. They're also not as precise and specific as people want them to be.    They're more like fuzzy targets. Remember: Polls have margins of error. So when someone has a 2-point lead, that's not a lead at all. If a poll has a 3 percentage-point margin of error, this means that candidate could have a 5-point lead or be losing by a point.   3. Look for transparency.    There has been a proliferation of not-so-great polls this cycle, some driven by AI, others without long track records and even a pollster exposed to be fake. Good pollsters show their work with detailed methodology pages. If you can't find a methodology, that's a red flag.   4. The quality of state-level polling is not very good.    With the decline of local journalism, there has been a decline in well-conducted, rigorous and frequent state polls. There is less money for those local outlets to pay for polling, which can be very expensive. So take those state poll averages with a grain of salt.   
   5. Go beyond the top lines.    Horse-race polling isn't the best use of polls. Polls are best when measuring attitudes over time to help inform us of how Americans are feeling and thinking about key issues. There is so much more underneath those top-line numbers, from job approval ratings and who is most motivated to vote, to which party is more trusted to handle the issues people care about most — and so much more.   The fact is that many of these races are expected to be close. Millions of votes are not yet cast, and anyone professing to know exactly what's going to happen is lying.   When you're looking at who's up and who's down, just remember that horse-race polling is like sprinkles on top of a bowl of ice cream. Lots of people like sprinkles, but if all you eat is the sprinkles, you just wind up with a mouth full of wax without ever getting to the good stuff.

schema.headline: Polls are a snapshot, and other helpful things to remember during the midterm elections

title: Democratic senator talks Trump's Russian diesel deal
description: NPR's Steve Inskeep speaks to Democratic Senator Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire about President Trump's deal for Russian diesel and his claim
body:
NPR's Steve Inskeep speaks to Democratic Senator Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire about President Trump's deal for Russian diesel and his claim of an "energy ceasefire" that did not materialize.   

    
        
          Transcript
        
    STEVE INSKEEP, HOST:  A bipartisan group of senators has objected to the president lifting sanctions on Russian energy. One of them is Senator Jeanne Shaheen, Democrat of New Hampshire, and we've reached her while she's on a congressional delegation visit to southeastern Europe. She's in Croatia. Senator, welcome.JEANNE SHAHEEN: Thank you. Nice to be with you.INSKEEP: Assuming this deal with Russia is authentic, what's wrong with buying Russian diesel?SHAHEEN: Well, first of all, there's no reason to believe this deal is authentic. But in 2022, Congress passed a law that expressly prohibited Russian imports. And it said the only way the administration could do that is if they first consulted with Congress and got Congress to agree to certain - if they agreed to the conditions that Congress set forth. This administration has not done that. And I question whether Russia even has any diesel to give to the United States. The fact is, Russia, because of the strikes against their energy infrastructure, has had long lines of cars queuing up and trucks queuing up to get - fill their gas tanks and fill diesel.And so this is an effort by the president to try and pretend that there's a reason why Americans are suffering from high gas and diesel prices that's not the war in Iran. And that's exactly why Americans are suffering. It's because this president started a war in Iran, and he has - he is being played by Vladimir Putin.INSKEEP: Is it necessary, though, to do something - for the United States to do something - given the administration's choice to go to war with Iran?SHAHEEN: Well, the administration should find a way to end the war in Iran. They should keep negotiating, and they're not willing to do that. They haven't been willing to stay at the table.INSKEEP: The president here has also blamed Ukraine for striking Russian energy facilities, suggesting that that is at least one factor in the high diesel prices. Do you blame Ukraine for taking that step?SHAHEEN: Absolutely not. The fact is Ukraine is trying to defend their country against these Russian attacks that are killing civilians by the hundreds on a weekly basis, that are undermining the country as it tries to move towards the West and democracy, and they're doing what they need to protect themselves. And the fact is, again, the president is looking for a scapegoat because he's in trouble with the American people because he's not done what he promised to do. He went to war in Iran when he said he wasn't going to engage in never-ending wars. He's done nothing about the high cost of living that people are facing.And so now people are seeing gas prices rise, diesel prices rise, grocery prices, rents and mortgages. Across the board, Americans are feeling the cost of this war in Iran, and President Trump is trying to blame someone else.INSKEEP: I'm curious about a detail we've heard. A Kremlin spokesman said in the last couple of days that Trump and Putin talked for an hour and that Trump would have loved to talk more. They seem to be great friends. Is there anything for the United States in that friendship?SHAHEEN: There is not. And what the president continues to deny is that the only way to get Vladimir Putin to come to the table and seriously negotiate on Ukraine is for the United States and Europe to continue to put pressure on him. And every time President Trump lifts the sanctions on gas and oil and allows Russia to continue to fund this illegal war in Ukraine, he just extends the war. And there are thousands of people who have died because this administration is unwilling to do something to put pressure on Vladimir Putin.INSKEEP: One other thing, Senator. Suppose you win the U.S. Senate - control of the Senate in November. Democrats are given a reasonable chance of prevailing in the Senate and a likelihood of prevailing in the House. Suppose you're in the majority in the Senate. How do you intend to approach the administration on these issues?SHAHEEN: Well, I think there's already bipartisan opposition. As you pointed out, this was bipartisan opposition that we sent to the administration against his proposal to allow Russian diesel to come into the United States. So there's bipartisan support for Ukraine. And hopefully our Republican colleagues, if they take a shellacking in November, will be willing to stand up to the president.INSKEEP: Do you think...SHAHEEN: Because the Democrats certainly will do that if we're in the majority.INSKEEP: Do you think that you'll have the numbers to make the Senate function - to be an effective check to the president? Because as you know, a narrowly divided Senate doesn't work very well.SHAHEEN: Well, the voters will decide that in November.INSKEEP: Senator Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire is traveling in Croatia. Thanks so much. Appreciate it.SHAHEEN: Thank you.INSKEEP: We'll note that we've invited multiple Republican lawmakers to join us this morning, and those invitations remain open for a future day.

title: Agents search Rep. Omar's D.C. home; DOJ says it's part of criminal investigation
description:
Federal agents search Rep. Ilhan Omar’s DC home, DOJ says it approved the warrant
    
            
                
                Tra
body:
Federal agents search Rep. Ilhan Omar’s DC home, DOJ says it approved the warrant
    
            
                
                Transcript
            
        
                Download
                
                
                    
                        
                            
                            Embed
                        
                        
                            <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-5998856/nx-s1-9961393" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
                        
                    
                
                
                  
                    
                    Transcript
                  
                
        
    



      
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                A Homeland Security Investigations agent gets in a car outside the Washington, D.C., residence of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., on Monday morning.
                
                    Luke Garrett/NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Luke Garrett/NPR
    

   
   Federal agents searched the Washington, D.C., home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., on Monday morning.   The Department of Justice said in a statement to NPR that agents with Homeland Security Investigations "executed a judicially authorized search warrant."   The warrant is part of an "ongoing federal criminal investigation," according to the DOJ.    Details about the investigation were confirmed by current and former federal officials with knowledge of the search who were not authorized to speak publicly.   One current official said this search is part of a multi-year probe that includes whistleblower complaints. A former official, who had previously been briefed on the matter, said the investigation deals with immigration fraud allegations.   
   Vice President JD Vance has previously alleged that Omar committed immigration fraud — something she denies.    Omar is a U.S. citizen who previously fled Somalia as a refugee.    By Monday afternoon, the congresswoman criticized the search of her D.C. home on social media.   "Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement," Omar posted on social media. "I will not be silenced."   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Federal agents walk away from the Washington, D.C., home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn.
                
                    Luke Garrrett/NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Luke Garrrett/NPR
    

   
   Several HSI agents could be seen walking near and around Omar's home on Monday.   Jackie Rogers, a spokesperson for the congresswoman, called the search an "outrageous abuse of power and an unprecedented escalation in the weaponization of federal law enforcement to target political enemies."   Sharon Jackson, 79, lives across the street from the congresswoman and said federal agents woke her up around 4:30 a.m. Monday morning.   "I got awakened by boom, boom, boom," Jackson said. "They were out here with a great big truck."   The search took place ahead of next month's midterm elections, in which Omar is seeking reelection.   The Department of Justice has had an internal rule that it shouldn't publicly probe election officials or candidates within 60 days of Election Day. It's meant to protect elections from a politicized use of law enforcement.   
   But the rule is not legally binding, and DOJ has in past years been inconsistent about it.   Senior DOJ leadership, including Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter, were consulted before the search and approved it, according to sources familiar but not authorized to discuss the case.   NPR's Ryan Lucas contributed to this report.

title: Voters here will decide whether to force cities to build cheaper, smaller homes
description: In North Braintree, Mass., larger lot si
body:
In North Braintree, Mass., larger lot sizes imposed decades ago have meant fewer homes, and bigger more expensive ones. Voters will decide whether to force cities to allow smaller homes on smaller lots.
                
                    Jennifer Ludden/NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Jennifer Ludden/NPR
    

   
   LEXINGTON, Mass. — Massachusetts is one of the most expensive states in the country, and it's easy to find people frustrated with high home prices.   "It's really hard to find housing, it's extremely expensive, and I can't afford to live alone," said renter Jamie Sharken, 34, as she walks her dog in Lexington, north of Boston and near where she shares a home with three others. "There's four of us in two bathrooms, definitely a run-down old house."   
   A massive housing shortage has pushed up prices. Sharken grew up in the state and would love to buy a home, but finds it hard to see how she could afford it.  She's not alone. "Most of my friends have so much debt from education," she said. "Just being able to save money to put a down payment on a house feels impossible these days."   She's heard about the ballot measure that aims to make housing more affordable by creating more starter homes on smaller lots.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Jamie Sharken, 34, grew up in Massachusetts but doubts she'll ever be able to afford a house there.  She supports a ballot measure that aims to create smaller starter homes.
                
                    Jennifer Ludden/NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Jennifer Ludden/NPR
    

   
   Cities and towns here and across the U.S. have set minimum lot sizes for single-family homes, many of them quite large. The measure would require them to allow homes on lots as small as 5,000 square feet, about the size of a basketball court. If it passes, Massachusetts would become the latest in a growing number of states to mandate such a zoning change amid a nationwide housing crunch.   The idea is to boost overall supply and override persistent, local "not in my backyard" opposition to new development. Critics bristle at the loss of local control and say the measure may not really help struggling first-time buyers.   
   But Sharken said encouraging smaller homes makes sense to her.   "There's so many homes that are empty with five, six, 10 bedrooms and one couple living there," she said. "I think it's time to share the wealth in terms of the space that we have and to have more housing for people."   An "existential crisis" generations in the making   To understand what's driving the zoning measure and how it would work, it helps to go back in time. Andrew Mikula, a housing economist leading the push for the ballot measure, takes me to a quiet street in North Braintree, about 10 miles south of Boston.   
   The block we stand on was built a century ago. Colonial and Cape Cod-style clapboard homes, with shutters and dormer windows, sit fairly close together. Some are about 1,000 square feet, with three bedrooms and 1.5 bathrooms. But this is a snapshot in time.   "With modern zoning, these homes are illegal to build today," Mikula said.   That's because after World War II, as suburbs exploded, cities across the country mandated bigger and bigger lot sizes for single-family homes only. The trend effectively banned apartments, duplexes or townhomes on large swaths of residential land and locked in economic and racial segregation. We see the change as we walk a couple of blocks down the street.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Andrew Mikula is a housing economist leading the push for smaller lot sizes. He stands on an older block in North Braintree, Mass., with smaller lots that would be illegal for new homes today.
                
                    Jennifer Ludden/NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Jennifer Ludden/NPR
    

   
   Suddenly, the yards are a lot bigger and so are the houses, with stylish arched windows and two-car garages. "You need to build a large McMansion just to justify the cost of assembling so much land," said Mikula. "So this is what you get."   In fact, most single-family zoning in the state requires at least an acre of land — about 40,000 square feet, or nearly the size of a football field without the end zones. That also means fewer homes get built. The ballot measure does not apply to Boston, which has its own zoning rules.   
   By the state's own data, expensive housing is fueling an exodus of working-age people. "And when we lose young workers and family members of people who already live here," Mikula said, "that not only separates extended families but also hurts our economy."   Retail, service, and healthcare workers who stay "just can't afford to live in the communities that they serve," said Jesse Kanson-Benanav, executive director at Abundant Housing Massachusetts.   He called the state's housing shortage "an existential crisis" that hits all generations. An estimated 400,000 young adults still live with their parents. Meanwhile, he said seniors struggle to maintain aging homes, "because we haven't built … moderate-sized and reasonably priced homes for them to downsize in their own community."   
   In recent years, Massachusetts lawmakers have forced cities to allow multifamily housing near transit stations and accessory dwelling units wherever single-family homes are allowed, and committed billions toward public and lower-income housing. Kanson-Benanav called the starter home ballot measure "one strategy among many" and hopes that if it passes, it will inspire lawmakers to do even more. Polling suggests broad support.   Even smaller homes can be pricey    Critics resent the prospect of a blanket state mandate and question whether it will produce truly affordable housing. To illustrate that concern, Lexington Select Board member Jill Hai took me to the backyard of a yellow clapboard two-story home with windows trimmed in red.   "We're looking at a beautiful home, I have to say," she said. "It's got beautiful hydrangeas."   This smallish lot is exactly what the ballot measure would allow, because the house was built in 1900. But it's been gut-renovated and expanded, and was on the market for nearly $1.3 million. "By the way, that is less than the median home value in Lexington, so it's a great deal!" Hai said with a laugh.   But it's hardly what most would consider a starter home. Just up the street, an even bigger new house on a small lot sold last year for more than $2 million.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                Adam Chapdelaine, with the Massachusetts Municipal Association, and Lexington Select Board member Jill Hai question how affordable smaller-lot homes would be and worry that a surge in new homes could strain local infrastructure.
                
                    Jennifer Ludden/NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Jennifer Ludden/NPR
    

   
   In the current market, at least in this affluent town, Hai didn't think the zoning change would be nearly as effective as other things Lexington has done, like creating rentals tied to people's income and using town-owned land to build affordable housing. She said local leaders know better what's needed — and she understands the housing crisis.   "My kids are 28 and 30, and they can't afford to come back to Lexington," she said.   
   Critics also worried that an unplanned surge in housing could strain schools, roads and other infrastructure.   The ballot measure only applies to places with water and sewer access, but "it doesn't speak to the water or sewer system capacity," said Adam Chapdelaine, executive director of the Massachusetts Municipal Association, which opposes the measure. Some already feel the need to expand capacity or are in the middle of planning for that.   "They are terrified that if this passes, that will completely upend those plans, or make it far more expensive and have to see those costs passed on to existing ratepayers," he said.   
   More states are mandating smaller lots   This year alone, lawmakers in Kansas, Maine and Idaho imposed smaller minimum lots to tackle housing costs. Texas did so last year. Most mandated even smaller sizes than Massachusetts' 5,000-square-foot ballot measure.   "Five thousand is a good start, and in our opinion it should be lower," said Tobias Peter, who tracks such policies at the conservative-leaning American Enterprise Institute.   
   He noted that zoning power has long been delegated to cities, but for years they've failed to produce enough housing to meet the need. Now, a growing number of states are taking back a power they've always had under the U.S. Constitution.   AEI has researched the impact of smaller lots on housing prices and supply, and found builders do produce more starter homes "if you allow them to build on smaller lots in areas that have lower land prices," said Peter.   But finding that cheaper land is hard near major cities like Boston. It's more likely in new developments farther out, Peter said, and the smaller the lots, the more affordable the price of the homes will be.   
            
        
            
            
            
        


    
        
                A century-old home in Lexington, Mass., sits on a smaller lot that's since been outlawed. But after a gut renovation and expansion, it was listed for more than $1 million.
                
                    Jennifer Ludden/NPR
                
                hide caption
            
            
    
        Jennifer Ludden/NPR
    

   
   So how much should a starter home cost? AEI defines it as less than four times a county's median household income. For the national median, which reached a record high in 2025 at $87,460, that would mean a starter home should cost less than $350,000.   But Massachusetts' housing shortage is so severe, Peter thought five or even six times the income made more sense. Given Massachusetts' high average income, that could mean $500,000 or more.   Is that really a starter home? "In Massachusetts it is!" he said.   "I wouldn't mind downsizing myself"   On a recent evening, about 30 people in a library conference room pledged allegiance to an American flag on a large screen. It was the start of a meeting of the Weymouth Democratic Town Committee to discuss this year's election ballot measures. The organizer noted he'd heard a lot of interest in the one on zoning.   
   The crowd was mostly older, with many homeowners, but opinions were mixed.   "I understand the problem. But I think they need to work a little harder to find a better solution," said Kathy Swain, who's lived in Weymouth all of her 70-plus years. She's very involved with local politics and does not like the idea of a state mandate.   "I just think that people in local communities need to have local authority, otherwise they're going to become more disengaged than they already are," she said.   
   A few feet away, Susan Donovan said she might be in favor of the measure, "because I wouldn't mind downsizing myself." Expensive housing makes that hard, too.   Donovan has been thinking about building a smaller place on her property and having the children move into the big house. "We don't need all the big land anymore," she said. "We don't want to mow it anymore, right? Small sounds good to me."

schema.headline: Voters here will decide whether to force cities to build cheaper, smaller homes
